data.title: CPTPP-ASEAN-EU meet: Stable trade, supply chain resilience in focus
data.description:
The European Union, the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) gathered in Vietnam to discuss economic ties and supply chain resilience.

Some of the 14 countries that were targeted with new U.S. tariffs this week were among the participants of the dialogue. These include the EU, Japan, Vietnam, Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia.

"In this time of global trade uncertainty, CPTPP parties and the EU are committed toreinforcing a stable and predictable trade environment," according to a joint statement from the blocs.

Notably, the EU and CPTPP announced a supply chain early warning network that aims to identify supply chain risks earlier, exchange information faster and coordinate responses to disruptions. The network will hold its first meeting in early 2027.

EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the network will help both blocs to "better anticipate disruptions, reduce vulnerabilities and support businesses and citizens who depend on open and reliable trade."

To note, the CPTPP is the successor to the Trans-Pacific Partnership, which was originally led by the U.S. President Trump withdrew from the Pacific Rim trade bloc in 2017.

The CPTPP now comprises the UK, Japan, Australia, Canada, Chile, Vietnam, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Singapore, Brunei and Peru.

Members of the CPTPP and ASEAN also resolved to strengthen supply chain resilience and global value chains through their collective actions, among other commitments.

Separately, the CPTPP agreed to start talks regarding the UAE, Indonesia ‌and the Philippines potentially joining the bloc.

data.title: Volkswagen drags rivals Mercedes, BMW into $1.2 billion India tax fight
data.description:
Key points:
  • Volkswagen says its India rivals also pay 10% duty on parts
  • Filing cites 2024 import data of BMW, Mercedes, Kia and others
  • Court to rule on Monday, likely only on whether 12-year look-back is allowed
  • Tariff investigations remain a sore point for foreign investors in India

By Aditi Shah and Aditya Kalra

Volkswagen has told an Indian court that tax authorities have wrongly singled it out over how it imports car parts at lower tariffs, alleging rivals Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Kia do the same, its latest salvo as it seeks to quash a $1.2 billion tax demand.

The German carmaker has been fighting since 2025 to quash the record tax demand over allegations it "deliberately" imported components at a 10% tariff and then assembled them into complete cars in India, evading the higher tariffs of around 30% applicable on car kits.

Volkswagen has denied the allegations, describing the case as a matter of "life and death" that could "wipe out" all of its investments in India, where it has just a 2% market share. The dispute coincides with the German carmaker's challenges back home due to worker disputes over pay, and falling sales in its key Chinese market.

After India accused VW of being the only carmaker indulging in such practices, the German company's unit in a non-public Mumbai court filing dated November 10 said "every manufacturer of comparable cars" follows the same "parts/components model" and pays duty at 10%.

If VW succeeds with its arguments about how its rivals import car parts, other carmakers could potentially face heightened scrutiny in the world's third-largest auto market.

TAX DEMAND 'DESERVES TO BE QUASHED'

"The contention that all other manufacturers paid duty at 30% while the petitioner alone paid 10% is unfortunate and factually incorrect," Volkswagen's India unit said in the filing, seen by Reuters, and being reported for the first time.

The tax demand "deserves to be quashed for requiring the petitioner alone to pay 30% duty while all other manufacturers pay 10%," it added.

To support its argument, VW attached a one-page table showing import shipment numbers of Mercedes , BMW, Hyundai's sister company Kia, Isuzu Motors and SAIC Motor's India unit JSW MG Motor, the filing showed.

VW's India unit, Skoda Auto Volkswagen India, declined to comment citing ongoing legal proceedings. Kia declined to comment on Volkswagen's submission, but said it imports car components in accordance with applicable laws.

The other rival carmakers it cited in the filing did not respond to Reuters queries, and neither did India's tax authorities.

In an October submission to the court, seen by Reuters, Indian tax authorities described VW's conduct as one of "fraud and subterfuge".

TARIFF DISPUTES LONG A SORE POINT FOR FOREIGN INVESTORS

Tariff disputes have long been a sore point for foreign investors in India, as investigations and lawsuits can drag on for years, triggering business uncertainty. Global liquor majors currently are sparring with New Delhi over the tariff rate on bulk Scotch imports, though Indian officials say they are only enforcing the law of the land.

In the VW dispute, India has alleged the carmaker shipped nearly complete Audi, Skoda and Volkswagen cars to its India plant but as individual parts and in separate consignments to avoid paying higher taxes applicable on car kits, and used internal software to manage such imports.

After VW initiated a court challenge months after receiving a tax demand in 2024, Indian authorities told the Mumbai judge that other carmakers were paying rightful duty on their parts imports.

VW SAYS IT IS BEING WRONGLY SINGLED OUT

VW is disputing that argument with its own analysis, its latest court filing showed.

BMW had 390,360 "major import shipments" of car components in 2024, while Mercedes had 80,972, all imported under the lower tariff rate category, VW said in its submission, without elaborating.

VW is of the view that such a high number of component imports by rivals are also then used to assemble cars, just like it does, and so the carmaker is being wrongly singled out by New Delhi, according to two people familiar with the matter.

However, a third person familiar with the dispute said for VW to succeed in its arguments, it will have to show that its rivals' imports were used to assemble complete vehicles.

The court in Mumbai will on Monday decide on Volkswagen's challenge, but the people familiar with the matter said it is likely the court will for now only rule on whether tax authorities could have gone back 12 years in scrutinising VW imports or not.

data.title: This investment strategist is 100% in cash - and warns that buying the Nasdaq dip is like catching a falling knife
data.description:
By Jules Rimmer

42 Macro strategist thinks the Fed is three moves away from neutral

A career spent catching knives will be a brief one, says 42 Macro's Darius Dale

Just because Nasdaq briefly entered bear-market territory this week, that's no reason in itself to buy stock, is the message from the head of one investment research service.

Darius Dale, founder and chief executive of the investment research boutique 42 Macro has advice for investors who think it is: "Research shows that if you try to make a career out of catching falling knives, you're not going to have a career for very long.'

For Dale, far better to "be the second investor in a confirmed trade, not the first in an unconfirmed."

Dale was articulating his extremely cautious opinions on the David Lin Report podcast, aired Thursday,. Opinions that are so cautious, his KISS model portfolio (standing for "Keep it Simple and Systematic") shifted into 80% cash at the end of September and has for the last few weeks actually been 100% cash.

Justifying this bearish stance he replied to Lin's suggestion that one might just buy stocks because they've declined so much, "that's just not what we do. We have a risk management system that's looking for signals to confirm" a move like that.

The main reason for Dale's extreme caution is that the Federal Reserve, for credibility's sake, needs to hike in December, and probably again in March to shore up its inflation-fighting credentials. "If they don't hike in December, they might as well close the institution," he says. Right now, Dale's models calculate the Fed is three 25-basis point hikes away from a policy that could be described as neutral.

The Fed is expected to tighten into the first half of 2027

It's not just inflation forcing rates higher. Dale's Wall Street contacts indicate to him that the hyperscalers (AMZN) (GOOG) (MSFT) may issue as much as $1 trillion in debt over the next few years, triple what they raised this year. That adds upward pressure on the cost of capital.

Dale cites many factors suggesting the economy is running too hot, highlighting supercore personal consumption expenditure at 4.2% year-over-year. It may take then, in Dale's opinion, until the second half of 2027 for the narrative to shift from a restrictive to a more accommodative approach, creating a policy tailwind to support equities, metals and bitcoin (BTCUSD).

As well as its KISS model, 42 Macro also runs a "Dr Mo" portfolio, representing a discretionary risk management overlay that interprets signals from 80 different factors, including rates, currencies, stocks and commodities. Late September, that model too suggested a reduction in beta - stocks that exaggerate market moves in any direction - and to move up the quality spectrum.

Dale is concerned that markets are having to digest a slowdown in the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, specifically identifying data centers as well as the situation with Nvidia (NVDA) and issues surrounding its chip sales. Yet, he observes earnings forecasts for 2027 are still at or near the cycle highs.

At some point, when markets are convinced about the direction of rates, the markets may well rip, Dale says and when they do the things to buy will be semiconductors SOX, Korea KR:180721, Taiwan XX:180909, base metals , bitcoin and other crypto currencies. For now, though, "the signals are not telling us to put on risk."

-Jules Rimmer

data.title: Slow bird flu season offers relief for Europe's poultry sector
data.description:
Key points:
  • Bird flu outbreaks by late November at lowest level in Europe since 2020, data shows
  • Infections in the following months led to one of the worst bird flu crises in Europe
  • Bird flu has led to the death of more than 100 million poultry in the past decade in Europe

By Sybille de La Hamaide

Bird flu is spreading in Europe at its slowest pace since 2020, raising hopes the EU's €27 billion ($30 billion) poultry industry can avoid past crises that killed millions of poultry, though history shows it could still flare up later this season.

Highly pathogenic avian influenza, commonly known as bird flu, has devastated poultry flocks worldwide, disrupting food supplies and pushing up prices. Cases in mammals, including dairy cows and farm workers in the United States, have also raised concerns that the virus could mutate and spread between humans.

By November 23, 51 outbreaks had been detected on farms in the EU and UK, according to data compiled by France's animal health surveillance body ESA. That compares with 330 at the same point last year and is the lowest since the 21 recorded by this time in 2020.

In the US, outbreaks have also remained relatively limited so far this autumn, with 88 outbreaks confirmed on poultry farms and backyard flocks between August and November 25, affecting 6 million birds, US government data showed. That compared to 177 outbreaks and 9.5 million birds a year earlier.

A slow start, however, does not guarantee a mild season.

The 2020/21 season began quietly but became Europe's second-worst bird flu crisis so far, with more than 22 million birds dying or culled.

"Avian influenza is really difficult to predict. So there is not a guarantee that being late now means that there might be a lower risk this time than other years," Rabobank poultry analyst Nan-Dirk Mulder said.

Bird flu outbreaks in the Northern Hemisphere usually rise during autumn and winter wild-bird migration and often ease in spring, though recent waves have sometimes persisted outside this pattern.

Poland, the EU's largest poultry producer, reported its first outbreak in six months last week at a turkey farm.

Other countries reporting outbreaks on farms this season include France, Germany, the UK, the Netherlands, Portugal, Sweden, Bulgaria and Italy. Some ordered that flocks be kept inside, to protect them from the virus.

"We are very vigilant. When it comes to avian influenza, we must stay very humble. But for now, we are not at all in the kind of crisis situation we faced one or two years ago," said Bruno Mousset, a director at France's largest poultry group LDC .

($1 = 0.9136 euros)

data.title: Germany's Monday power price jumps on heating demand, below-normal wind
data.description:
The German spot electricity contract for Monday delivery rose on Friday, as cold weather was expected to keep heating demand high and wind output was forecast below the seasonal average.

  • The German baseload spot electricity contract (TRDEBD3) rose 35.0% to €263 ($289) per megawatt hour at 0950 GMT, LSEG data showed

  • The French equivalent contract (TRFRBD3) was untraded

  • German wind power generation is forecast to rise 3.4 GW from Friday to 15.2 GW on Monday, but remains 9.6 GW below the average

  • French wind output is projected to rise 0.1 GW to 3.8 GW, which is 4.6 GW less than the average, the data showed

  • "German wind output stays moderate ... while there are also very weak levels in France," analysts at Engie's EnergyScan said in a note, adding that solar output remained limited by snow and fog

  • Solar power generation in Germany is expected to fall 1.2 GW to 2.1 GW, while French solar output is seen down 0.1 GW at 1.9 GW

  • Consumption in Germany is expected to rise 0.6 GW to 65.9 GW, while French consumption is seen down 0.5 GW at 65.4 GW, LSEG data showed

  • French nuclear availability fell 4 percentage points to 73% of total capacity

  • Along the curve, the French 2027 baseload contract (TRFRBD3) fell 1.6% to €113.9/MWh, LSEG data showed

  • The equivalent German contract (TRDEBYc1) was down 0.9% at €143.25/MWh

  • Mind Energy analysts said they expected the German front-year contract to fall alongside gas prices on Friday

  • European wholesale gas prices fell, driven by milder temperature forecasts and higher Norwegian supply

  • The European carbon market's benchmark contract edged up 0.7% to €84.75 a metric ton

($1 = 0.9107 euros)

data.title: SAP seeks to cut sizeable number of jobs, sources say
data.description:
German business software company SAP is preparing to cut a sizeable number of jobs, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters on Friday.

The works council has not yet been informed about the plans, said one of the sources.

Bloomberg News reported late on Thursday that SAP is considering cutting at least 10,000 jobs in an AI-driven restructuring, citing people familiar with the matter.

CEO Christian Klein and Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam indicated at investor events in recent weeks that a reduction of the group's workforce of more than 110,000 was on the cards.

In early 2024, the group said it would review 8,000 jobs but cutbacks in slow-growing businesses have since been offset by new hires in more dynamics areas.

Recent moves have pointed to a more cost-conscious approach. An SAP executive told Reuters last month the company was replacing some expensive AI models powering its products with cheaper alternatives.
